common_name: Moerloosei Flowering Quince (Apple Blossom Flowering Quince)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or bare-root stock in spring or fall in any well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; give this older, larger-growing cultivar plenty of room since it is more vigorous and upright than most modern compact selections.

directions: Raised in Belgium in the 1860s, 'Moerloosei' is one of the oldest named flowering quince cultivars still in commerce, prized for large, semi-double flowers in soft pink shading to white at the petal base, closely mimicking apple blossom and giving rise to its common trade name. Bloom appears on bare, thorny stems in late winter to early spring well ahead of the foliage, followed by small, hard, aromatic yellow-green fruit useful for jelly or preserves. It tolerates poor, clay, or alkaline soil once established and blooms on old wood, so any shaping cuts should follow immediately after flowering to preserve next year's buds.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to part shade; site it where its eventual large size and stiff, spiny branching will not crowd walkways or smaller companion shrubs.

directions: Native to central and western China, Chaenomeles cathayensis is the largest and most tree-like species in the genus, forming a stiff, densely thorny large shrub or small tree distinct from the true Chinese quince (Pseudocydonia sinensis). Its white to pale pink flowers, often flushed rose at the base, open in early to mid spring and are followed by large, hard, ribbed, green-to-yellow fruit that can reach 4 to 6 inches long, among the biggest of any flowering quince. Highly drought-tolerant and adaptable once established, it is grown more for its dramatic scale, fruit, and thorny wildlife cover than for the profusion of bloom typical of C. speciosa and C. x superba cultivars.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in any well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; its dense, spreading habit suits mixed borders, low hedging, or training flat against a sunny wall.

directions: An RHS Award of Garden Merit selection raised at the historic Knap Hill Nursery in England, 'Knap Hill Scarlet' bears an especially heavy, long-lasting display of bright orange-scarlet flowers on a dense, wide-spreading, thorny frame in late winter into early spring, before the leaves emerge. Small, hard, aromatic fruit follows and can be cooked into jelly or preserves, though it is grown chiefly for its vivid, reliable spring color. Thriving in poor, clay, sandy, or alkaline soils once established, it blooms on old wood, so prune, if needed, only right after flowering to avoid sacrificing the next season's buds.

common_name: Simonii Flowering Quince (Low Brick-Red Flowering Quince)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in any well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; its low, ground-hugging habit makes it useful as a thorny, colorful spring groundcover or bank planting rather than a specimen shrub.

directions: Introduced in France in the 1880s and still grown for its distinctly low, spreading, near-prostrate habit, 'Simonii' is one of the flattest-growing flowering quince selections available, rarely exceeding two feet tall while spreading considerably wider. It produces semi-double, brick-red flowers in dense clusters directly on the thorny stems in late winter to early spring, followed by small yellow-green fruit suitable for jelly. Tough and drought-tolerant once established in average or poor soil, it blooms on old wood, so any pruning to control spread should be done immediately after flowering.
